constraints: nums is a sorted array rotated between 0 and n − 1 times.

examples.explain: 8 would sit between 7 and 9, but it isn't there.

followUp: What breaks if values can repeat? Try [1, 0, 1, 1, 1] with target 0.
hints: Split the array at mid. With only one drop in the whole array, at least one half has no drop at all.
A sorted half tells you its range from its two ends. Is target inside that range?
If nums[lo] <= nums[mid], the left half is sorted: go left only if nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid]. Otherwise the right half is sorted: go right only if nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi].

insight.oneLiner: At every split one half is sorted; check whether target fits its range, and discard whichever half can't hold it.
insight.pattern: Binary search with a sorted half

recall.a: nums[lo] <= nums[mid]. The <= matters when lo == mid (a one-element left half).
recall.q: How do you know the left half is sorted?

recall.a: If target is within the sorted half's endpoints, search it; otherwise search the other half.
recall.q: Once you know which half is sorted, how do you choose a side?

recall.a: First binary-search the rotation point (the minimum), then binary-search the one sorted run that can contain target.

insight.why: A rotated sorted array has a single drop, so mid splits it into one sorted half and one that may contain the drop. A sorted half's ends bound its values, so 'is target in here?' is two comparisons - and either answer discards half the range.

oneLiner: At every split one half is sorted; check whether target fits its range, and discard whichever half can't hold it.

pitfalls.explain: When lo == mid, the left half is just nums[mid], which is trivially sorted - but nums[lo] < nums[mid] says it isn't. Use nums[lo] <= nums[mid].
pitfalls.title: Misjudged a one-element left half

pitfalls.explain: The target is there. Check the sorted half's bounds carefully: the left half is nums[lo] <= target < nums[mid], the right half nums[mid] < target <= nums[hi]. And loop while lo <= hi.
pitfalls.title: Returned -1 for a target that's in the array

pitfalls.explain: Only return mid after checking nums[mid] == target.
pitfalls.title: Returned an index for a missing target

solutions.idea: Check each value. Correct, but O(n) - the rotation doesn't matter to it, and neither does the sorting.
solutions.name: Linear scan

solutions.idea: Binary-search the index of the minimum, which splits nums into two sorted runs. Target's value says which run it must be in; binary-search that one.
solutions.name: Find the rotation point, then search one run

footnotes.text: One half of every split is sorted, because the array has only one drop. Check the sorted half: its ends tell you instantly whether target is inside it. If not, it's in the other half.

solutions.idea: At each mid, one half is sorted. If target lies within that half's endpoints, search it; otherwise search the other half. One loop, one pass.
solutions.name: One binary search, trusting the sorted half

class Solution:
    def search(self, nums: List[int], target: int) -> int:
statement:
`nums` holds **distinct** integers that were sorted in increasing order and then rotated: a prefix was moved, in order, to the back (possibly an empty prefix). `[1, 3, 5, 7, 9]` rotated by 3 is `[7, 9, 1, 3, 5]`.

Return the index of `target` in `nums`, or `-1` if it isn't there. Your solution must run in **O(log n)** time.
title: Search in Rotated Sorted Array
